planting.note: Tuck divisions or pot-grown plants into crevices of lean, acidic, sharply drained scree or stone-wall soil in partial shade, keeping the rootzone cool and free of lime.

directions: This small European mountain fern produces two distinct frond types each season: bright green, finely divided sterile fronds resembling curly parsley, and narrower, more upright fertile fronds that turn rusty brown as spores mature in late summer. It is native to acidic screes, mountain stone walls, and rocky banks, so it resents limy soil and heavy clay, performing best in a lean, gritty, humus-poor mix with sharp drainage. Site it in a cool, partly shaded rock garden pocket or crevice where its tufted habit can be appreciated at close range, and avoid disturbing the slow-spreading rhizome once established.

planting.note: Wedge small divisions into moist, calcareous rock crevices or a gritty, humus-rich pocket in deep shade, mimicking the damp limestone ledges this diminutive fern favors in the wild.

directions: One of North America's smallest and most delicate ferns, this species forms loose, thin mats of pale green, once- or twice-divided fronds only a few inches tall, native to damp, shaded limestone and dolomite cliffs, seeps, and talus slopes across the northern United States and Canada. Unlike most garden ferns it favors alkaline, calcium-rich rock crevices with constant seepage moisture rather than ordinary humus-rich woodland soil, and it goes dormant quickly if the rock face it inhabits dries out. It suits a shaded limestone rock garden, a damp wall crevice, or a trough planted with calcareous grit, and spreads very slowly, so patience is needed between divisions.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; grow outdoors year-round only in mild, nearly frost-free gardens, otherwise as a container or greenhouse fern.

directions: Native to southern Africa, this cliff brake forms clumps of once- or twice-divided, glossy mid-green fronds carried on the dark, wiry stipes typical of the genus, giving it a tidier, more lush appearance than many of its drier-growing North American relatives. It tolerates a wider range of moisture than most Pellaea species and prefers consistently moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil rather than the lean rocky grit favored by desert cliff brakes. Outside nearly frost-free climates it is best grown as a shaded patio or greenhouse container fern, overwintered indoors away from cold drafts. Divide congested clumps in spring and avoid letting the soil dry out completely between waterings.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from hard frost; well suited to shaded rock crevices and the base of trees in mild climates.

directions: Native to eastern Australia, New Zealand, and the southwest Pacific, sickle fern takes its common name from the gently curved, leathery pinnae strung along wiry, dark stipes, giving each frond a distinctive scythe-like outline unlike the more delicate lacy texture of many shade ferns. It is typically found growing in forest understory, among rock outcrops, or at the base of tree trunks, tolerating drier shade once established better than many fine-textured ferns. In mild, frost-light climates it makes a tidy, slow-spreading evergreen accent for a shaded border or rockery; elsewhere it is best treated as a protected courtyard or container specimen. Divide established clumps in spring only occasionally, as growth is slow.

planting.note: Press small plantlets or rhizome sections onto moist, humus-topped rock, bark, or well-drained soil in partial to full shade; keep consistently moist until the creeping rhizome anchors itself.

directions: This East Asian fern creeps along rocks, tree bark, and shaded ground on a thin, wiry rhizome studded with tiny, rounded, coin-like evergreen fronds only an inch or so tall, forming a flat, moss-like mat rather than an upright clump. It is a favorite in Japanese gardens for softening stones, tree bases, and low walls in deep shade, clinging tightly to its support with fine roots along the rhizome. Growth is slow but steady in consistently moist, humus-rich conditions, and established mats need little care beyond occasional watering during dry spells. Propagate by detaching and pinning down rooted sections of rhizome in spring.
